## Basic R Objects and Operations


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# create a vector
x <- 1:10
x <- seq(30, 3, by = -2)
a <- c(66.32, 69.87, 70.12, 90.37, 50.08, 61.20, 65.00, 57.65)
d <- a[1]
a[1] <- 85.34

mean(a)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 68.70375
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ma <- mean(a)

# read a vector of numbers from a file (assumes files exist)
# x <- scan("data/numbers.txt")
# x2 <- scan("data/number2.txt")

# one can also read number without saving to a file
y <- scan(text = "7  8  9 10 11 12 13 13 14 17 17 45")

# create a matrix
A <- matrix(0, 4, 2)
A <- matrix(1:8, 4, 2)
A
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

[1,]    1    5
[2,]    2    6
[3,]    3    7
[4,]    4    8
```

:::

```{.r .cell-code}
D <- matrix(a, 4, 2, byrow = TRUE)
D <- matrix(1:8, 2, 4)

```

## Data Manipulation and Data Table

### Pipe Operations

The native pipe `|>` takes the value on its left and passes it as the **first argument** to the function on its right. `x |> f()` is just another way of writing `f(x)`, and pipes can be chained so that the output of one step feeds into the next.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, NA)

# without the pipe
sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 15
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
log(sum(x, na.rm = TRUE), base = 10)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1.176091
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
round(exp(log(sum(x, na.rm = TRUE), base = 10)), digits = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 3.24
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# the same computations written with the pipe, read left to right
x |> sum(na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 15
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
x |> sum(na.rm = TRUE) |> log(base = 10)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1.176091
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
x |> sum(na.rm = TRUE) |> log(base = 10) |> exp() |> round(digits = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 3.24
```


:::
:::


Extra arguments still work as usual — they just go after the piped-in first argument. Each `|>` step below passes its result on as the *first* argument only; any other arguments (`na.rm`, `trim`, `decreasing`, `digits`) are supplied by name at each step:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
c(1, 4, 9, 16, NA) |>
  sum(na.rm = TRUE) |>
  sqrt() |>
  round(digits = 1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 5.5
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
c(5, 1, NA, 3, 9) |>
  sort(decreasing = TRUE, na.last = NA) |>
  mean(trim = 0.1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 4.5
```


:::
:::


When the piped-in value needs to land in an argument other than the first, use the placeholder `_` to mark where it goes (the named argument holding `_` must be spelled out):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# without the pipe: mtcars is the *data* argument to lm(), not the first argument
lm(mpg ~ disp, data = mtcars)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

Call:
lm(formula = mpg ~ disp, data = mtcars)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)         disp  
   29.59985     -0.04122  
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# with the placeholder, mtcars |> lm(mpg ~ disp, data = _) sends mtcars to `data`
mtcars |> lm(mpg ~ disp, data = _)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

Call:
lm(formula = mpg ~ disp, data = mtcars)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)         disp  
   29.59985     -0.04122  
```


:::
:::


### Modern Data Manipulation using `dplyr`


The `dplyr` package and the native pipe (`|>`) make modifying, subsetting, and summarizing data frames much cleaner than base R.

### Displaying Large Datasets with a Scroll Bar

When working with large datasets, printing the entire dataframe to your HTML document takes up too much vertical space and can slow down the browser. We can use the `gt` package to create a fixed-height, scrollable window, so HTML readers can scroll through the **full** dataset. A static, non-HTML render (e.g. Typst/PDF) has no scrollbar, so there we show only the head of the data instead.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(gt)

# Display the FULL dataset inside a scrollable box (HTML only)
agpop |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Agricultural Population Data",
    subtitle = "Scroll to view more rows"
  ) |>
  tab_options(
    container.height = px(400),   # Restricts the table height to 400 pixels
    container.overflow.y = TRUE   # Enables the vertical scroll bar
  )
```

### Advanced Tables with `gt`

The `gt` package also allows you to create highly customized, publication-ready tables. Below, we summarize five variables of the `agpop` dataset by region, computing both the mean and the variance of each, and create a table featuring spanning headers across multiple columns and complex mathematical LaTeX symbols in the column labels.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# The five variables we want to summarize
vars_of_interest <- c("acres92", "acres87", "farms92", "largef92", "smallf92")

# Create a summary dataset by region: mean and variance of each variable,
# filtering out rows where any of the five variables is missing (-99)
ag_summary <- agpop |>
  filter(if_all(all_of(vars_of_interest), ~ .x != -99)) |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarize(
    across(
      all_of(vars_of_interest),
      list(mean = ~mean(.x), var = ~var(.x)),
      .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
    )
  )
ag_summary
```

The spanners above group columns by **statistic** (all means together, all variances together). We can instead reorder the columns with `select()` and group them by **variable**, so each variable's mean and variance sit side by side under their own spanning header.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ag_summary |>
  select(region,
         acres92_mean, acres92_var,
         acres87_mean, acres87_var,
         farms92_mean, farms92_var,
         largef92_mean, largef92_var,
         smallf92_mean, smallf92_var) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Regional Summary: Mean and Variance of Five Variables",
    subtitle = "Grouped by variable"
  ) |>
  # One spanning header per variable, covering its mean and variance columns
  tab_spanner(label = md("**acres92**"),  columns = c(acres92_mean, acres92_var)) |>
  tab_spanner(label = md("**acres87**"),  columns = c(acres87_mean, acres87_var)) |>
  tab_spanner(label = md("**farms92**"),  columns = c(farms92_mean, farms92_var)) |>

  tab_spanner(label = md("**smallf92**"), columns = c(smallf92_mean, smallf92_var)) |>
  # The spanner already names the variable, so the column labels can stay generic
  cols_label(
    region        = md("**Region**"),
    acres92_mean  = md("$\\bar y$"),
    acres92_var   = md("$s^2$"),
    acres87_mean  = md("$\\bar y$"),

  ) |>
  fmt_number(
```

### Saving and Inserting External Plots

Sometimes you need to export a high-resolution plot for a journal submission or a presentation. You can save a plot directly to your computer by opening a "graphics device" (like `pdf()`, `png()`, or `jpeg()`), running your plot code, and then closing the device with `dev.off()`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 1. Open the PNG device with high resolution (res = 300)
# Note: When increasing resolution, you must also scale up the width/height in pixels or specify units in inches.
png("agpop_scatter_highres.png", width = 6, height = 4, units = "in", res = 300)

plot(agpop$acres87, agpop$acres92, main = "1992 vs 1987 Acreage")
abline(a = 0, b = 1, col = "red")

dev.off()
```
:::


Once the file is saved in your project folder, you can insert it back into your Quarto document at any time using the `knitr` package.

### Advanced Visualization with `ggplot2`

While base R graphics are useful for quick checks, `ggplot2` provides a powerful grammar of graphics for complex visuals. Below, we generate a histogram of log-transformed 1992 acreages, overlaying both an empirical density curve and a theoretical normal distribution curve.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(ggplot2)

# Modern data prep with pipes
ag_clean <- agpop |>
  filter(acres92 != -99, acres92 > 0) |>
  mutate(log_acres = log(acres92))

# Calculate parameters for the theoretical normal curve
mean_log <- mean(ag_clean$log_acres)
sd_log <- sd(ag_clean$log_acres)

ggplot(ag_clean, aes(x = log_acres)) +
  # 1. Base Histogram mapped to density (instead of count)
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 30, 
                 fill = "steelblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.7) +
  # 2. Empirical Density Curve (Dark Red)
  geom_density(color = "darkred", linewidth = 1.2) +
  # 3. Theoretical Normal Curve (Black, Dashed)
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, 
                args = list(mean = mean_log, sd = sd_log), 
                color = "black", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Log(Acres92)",
    subtitle = "Histogram with Empirical Density (Red) and Normal Fit (Black Dashed)",
    x = "Log of 1992 Farm Acreage",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Create your own function


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## data is a matrix or data.frame
means_col <- function(data)
{
    n <- ncol(data)
    cmeans <- rep(NA, n)
    for (j in 1:n)
    {
        cmeans[j] <- mean(data[,j], na.rm = TRUE)
    }
    cmeans
}
```
:::




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(gt)

## apply custom function (using dplyr to select numeric columns first)
agpop_numeric <- agpop |> select(3:13)
custom_means <- means_col(agpop_numeric)

## apply R built-in function
builtin_means <- colMeans(agpop_numeric, na.rm = TRUE)

## Create a data frame to compare the results
comparison_df <- data.frame(
  Variable = colnames(agpop_numeric),
  Custom_Function = custom_means,
  Built_in = builtin_means
)

## Display the comparison as a clean table
comparison_df |> 
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(
    title = "Comparing Mean Calculations",
    subtitle = "Custom Function vs. Base R colMeans()"
  ) |> 
  cols_label(
    Variable = md("**Variable**"),
    Custom_Function = md("**Custom `means_col()`**"),
    Built_in = md("**Base `colMeans()`**")
  ) |> 
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(Custom_Function, Built_in),
    decimals = 2
  )
```
